MATH2050 Mathematical Analysis I

To formally understand what is real number and do analysis on them, we must axiomatically deduce everything we use in daily life without thinking. What are the underlying principles in the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$?

Order Structures

Partially Ordered Set

To start with, we must clarify the notations used in (partial) ordering. As the wordings looks quite the same if you consult common sense, but not mathematically. Consider the poset $(X, \le)$ where $\le$ is reflexive ($x \le x$), anti-symmetric ($x \le y \land y \le x \implies x = y$) and transitive ($x \le y \land y \le z \implies x \le z$) on the ground set $X$. For an arbitrary subset $S \subset X$, what can we define?

First of all, the upper bound of $S$ is intuitively defined as $\{ x \in X: y \le x \text{ for all } y \in S \}$. Note that the upper bound of $S$ is not required to be in $S$; for example, we say $2$ is an upper bound $[1, 2)$ although $2 \not\in [1, 2)$. A set is said to be bounded above if the set of upper bound is non-empty. The maximum of $S$ is defined more strictly as $\{ x \in S: y \le x \text{ for all } y \in S \}$, which is required to be in $S$ itself. In that sense, $\max \ [1, 2)$ does not exist. Note that if maximum of $S$ exists, it must also be unique, since if $M_1$ and $M_2$ are both maximum of $S$ then $M_1 \le M_2$ and $M_2 \le M_1$, then by anti-symmetric of partial order we have $M_1 = M_2$. We say the supremum of $S$ as the lowest upper bound of $S$, that is, the minimum of the set of upper bounds for $S$. Since $\sup S$ is the minimum of some set, it is unique if exists as well. For example, $\sup \ [1, 2) = 2$. Finally, we define the maximal elements of $S$ as $\{ x \in S : x \le y \text{ for no } y \in S \}$.

Obviously, we can define lower bound, bounded below, minimum, infimum and minimal elements in a similar manner as upper bound, bounded above, maximum, supremum and maximal elements respectively. Although these namings look strikely similar, they carry different meanings, which one shall be aware of.

Order Structure of $\mathbb{R}$

We all know that $\mathbb{R}$ is with total order, partial order where every two elements are comparable. What so special about the order structure of $\mathbb{R}$? Turns out it is related to supremum (infimum). By writing $L = \sup S$, we means (1) $L \ge x$ for all $x \in S$, and (2) if $L' \ge x$ for all $x \in S$, then $L' \ge L$. Similarly, by writing $\ell = \inf S$, we mean (1) $\ell \le x$ for all $x \in S$ and (2) if $\ell' \le x$ for all $x \in S$, then $\ell' \le \ell$. Clearly by defining $-S = \{ -x \in \mathbb{R} : x \in S \}$, we have $\inf (-S) = - \sup S$.

In $\mathbb{R}$, there is another equivalent $\varepsilon$-characterisation for supremum (and infimum): $L = \sup S$ if (1) $L \ge x$ for all $x \in S$ and (2) for all $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there exists $x \in S$ where $x \gt L - \varepsilon$. The version for infimum is just direct translation. One may wonder why these two definitions are equivalent? A way of thinking is like this: the first definition says $L$ is the minimum of the set of upper bounds (smaller than any other upper bound), while the second definition says $L$ is a minimal element of the set of upper bounds (no smaller element can be upper bound). Since $\mathbb{R}$ has total order, minimal element is equivalent to a minimum!

For the set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$, we have the axiom of completeness: Every bounded-above non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ always has a supremum. This is non as a trivial statement as it looks, since supremum is defined as the minimum of the upper bounds, which the minimum of an arbitrary set (for example $(1, 2]$) does not necessarily exists! However, interestingly, if the non-empty set is specified as a upper bound, then somehow we think the minimum always exists. From the word choice of axiom, we will actually take this for granted - and everything else will be proven based on the axiom of completeness.

Noting the useful lemma that $e \le f \iff \forall \varepsilon \gt 0, \ e \lt f + \varepsilon$ and with the $\varepsilon$-characterisation of supremum, one may prove simple equalities like $\sup (A + B) = \sup A + \sup B$ whenever $\sup A$ and $\sup B$ exists. One may also prove the Achimede's Property (AP) that for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x \lt n$; Suppose otherwise, then $\mathbb{N}$ is upper bounded and so $\sup \mathbb{N}$ exists in $\mathbb{R}$ by axiom of completeness. Thus, there exists $m \in \mathbb{N}$ where $m \gt \sup \mathbb{N} - 1$ and $m + 1 \gt \sup \mathbb{N}$, contradiction. As a corollary, we have $\inf \{ n^{-1} : n \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \} = 0$.

Finally, we discuss briefly the notion of density. A set $S \subset \mathbb{R}$ is dense if and only if for all set $a \lt b \in \mathbb{R}$, we have $(a, b) \cap S \ne \varnothing$. One may show that the set of rational numbers $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$: By picking $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{n} \lt b - a$ by AP and also get $na \lt m$ where $m \in \mathbb{N}$ minimal by AP, we have $a \lt \frac{m}{n} \lt b$. Similarly, $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{Q}^c$ is also dense in $\mathbb{R}$ by simply considering $\mathbb{Q} \sqrt{2}$, which the existence of $\sqrt{2}$ is once again guaranteed by the axiom of completeness as $\inf \{ x \gt 0 : x^2 \le 2 \}$.

Sequences

A sequence on real numbers, denoted as $(x_n)$, can be considered as a function $x: \mathbb{Z}^+ \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. As it turns out, sequences are quite useful in terms of real analysis.

Convergence

We say a sequence $(x_n)$ convergent iff $$ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists N \in \mathbb{N} \quad \forall n \ge N \quad |x_n - L| \lt \varepsilon $$ Where $L = \lim x_n$ is called the limit of the sequence $(x_n)$. Alternatively we can also write $(x_n) \rightarrow L$. Intuitively speaking, it means that for every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there exists a tail of the sequence such that the "fluctuation" is smaller than $\varepsilon$. If a sequence is not convergent, we say it is divergent.

Clearly convergence implies boundedness, and if $\lim x_n = a$ and $\lim y_n = b$, then $\lim (x_n + y_n) = a + b$, $\lim (x_n y_n) = ab$ and $\lim \left(\frac{x_n}{y_n} \right) = \frac{a}{b}$ whenever division is well defined. We may also prove the comparison theorem that if $x_n \le y_n$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $(x_n) \rightarrow L_x$ and $(y_n) \rightarrow L_y$, then $L_x \le L_y$. Similarly, we have the squeeze theorem: for $x_n \le z_n \le y_n$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $(x_n), (y_n) \rightarrow L$, then $(z_n) \rightarrow L$ as well. All the above can be proven base on the $\varepsilon$-characterisation.

Interestingly, $L = \sup S$ iff $L$ is upper bound of $S$ and there exists a sequence $(x_n) \subset S$ where $(x_n) \rightarrow L$! One may note that both sides are just reformulations of the $\varepsilon$-characterisation for supremum with say $\varepsilon_n = \frac{1}{n}$. Finally, let's introduce two useful theorems.

We say a sequence $(x_n)$ is increasing if $x_n \le x_{n + 1}$ for all $n$, and strictly increasing if the inequality is strict. We similarly define decreasing and strictly decreasing, and finally, a sequence is called monotone if it is either increasing or decreasing. With these definitions in mind, we can introduce the monotone convergence theorem - If a sequence $(x_n)$ is monotone and bounded, then it is also convergent, which the limit is exactly the supremum (for increasing sequence) or infimum (for decreasing sequence). This is also implicitly implied by the axiom of completeness.

Finally, we have the nested interval theorem. For a sequence of nested intervals $$ I_1 \supseteq I_2 \supseteq \cdots \supseteq I_n \supseteq \cdots $$ Where $I_n = [a_n, b_n]$ are closed intervals, then the intersection $\bigcap \{ I_n \} \ne \varnothing$. Why? Note that $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ are monotone and bounded so they are convergent, while by comparison theorem we have $\lim a_n \le \lim b_n$. Hence, any $c \in \mathbb{R}$ where $\lim a_n \le c \le \lim b_n$ we have $c \in \bigcap \{ I_n \}$. Clearly for the special case where $\lim a_n = \lim b_n$, we have $\bigcap \{ I_n \} = \{ c \}$.

Subsequence

Formally speaking, a subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ is derived from the sequence $(x_k)$ where $n_k : \mathbb{Z^+} \rightarrow \mathbb{Z^+}$ is an increasing sequence. Turns out, the convergence of subsequences are interesting as well.

Trivially, if $(x_n)$ converges to the limit $L$, then every subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ converges to the same limit $L$ as well. What if $(x_n)$ does not converges? In fact, we can always find a convergent subsequence as long as $(x_n)$ is bounded by the Bolzano-Weierstrass Theorem! Assume $X = \{ x_n : n \in \mathbb{N} \}$ is infinite since otherwise we are done. Then, let $S := \{ x \in \mathbb{R} : (x, \infty) \cap X \text{ is infinite} \}$. Since $X$ is bounded, $S$ is bounded and $\sup S$ is well-defined. Thus, $(\sup S - \varepsilon, \sup S + \varepsilon)$ always contain infinite elements of $\{ x_n \}$, and so we can find a subsequence of $(x_n)$ that converges to $\sup S$. Alternatively, Bolzano-Weierstrass can also be proven by nested interval theorem by essentially binary search on the set with infinite number of elements.

The first proof of B-W inspires us for defining the limit supremum / infimum for (bounded) sequences, $\lim \sup x_n = \overline{\lim} x_n = \lim \sup \{ x_k : k \ge n \}$, and $\lim \inf x_n = \underline{\lim} x_n = \lim \inf \{ x_k : k \ge n \}$. Both of them always exists, since say for $\overline{\lim} x_n$, $\sup \{ x_k : k \ge n\}$ is always bounded and decreasing, and so it is convergent! Clearly we have $(x_n)$ convergent iff $\overline{\lim} x_n = \underline{\lim} x_n$, and we have the simple relations $\overline{\lim}(-x_n) = -\underline{\lim}(x_n)$, $\overline{\lim}(ax_n) = a(\overline{\lim}x_n)$ for $a \ge 0$ and $\underline{\lim} x_n + \underline{\lim} y_n \le \underline{\lim} (x_n + y_n) \le \overline{\lim} (x_n + y_n)$, all which can be proven from definitions.

Sequentially Compact Set

Another important definition to be gone through is the notion of compactness. For a set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$, it is called sequentially compact if for all $(x_n) \subset A$, there exists a convergent subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ such that $\lim x_{n_k} \in A$. Note that Bolzano-Weierstrass implies that any closed and bounded intervals are sequentially compact. In $\mathbb{R}$, how can we characterise all the sets that are sequentially compact?

Let's delve slightly into topology. Let $A \subset \mathbb{R}$. Then $\ell \in \mathbb{R}$ is a limit point or cluster point of $A$ iff $$ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists a \in A \quad 0 \lt |\ell - a| \lt \varepsilon $$ Where the set of all cluster points is denoted as $D(A)$. We say the set $A$ is closed whenever $D(A) \subseteq A$, and $\overline{A} = A \cup D(A)$ the closure of $A$. Of course we can define $D_\ell(A)$ and $D_r(A)$ be the cluster points when approaches from left and right respectively. For instances, $D((0, 1)) = [0, 1]$, $D_\ell((0, 1)) = (0, 1]$ and $D_r((0, 1)) = [0, 1)$.

Let us look at some properties for closed sets. We see $\overline{A}$ is closed, since for $(x_n) \subset \overline{A}$ convergent, we can find $(y_n) \subset A$ with the same limit where $|x_n - y_n| \lt \frac{1}{n}$, while $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ is closed iff $\overline{A} = A \cup D(A) = A$. We also have the equivalent conditions $$ \begin{align*} & z \in \overline{A} \\ \iff & \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists a \in A \quad |z - a| \lt \varepsilon \\ \iff & \exists (x_n) \subset A \quad (x_n) \rightarrow z \end{align*} $$ While if $A \subseteq B$ where $B$ is closed, then $\overline{A} \subseteq B$. Really finally, $\overline{A} = \mathbb{R}$ if and only if $A$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$. All these can be deduced from the definitions.

Back to the original topic. In fact, a set $A$ is sequentially compact iff $A$ is closed and bounded. First assume $A$ is sequentially compact. If $A$ is unbounded, then we can simply find a sequence $(x_n)$ such that $\Vert x_n - x_1 \Vert \rightarrow \infty$ and so any subsequence of $(x_n)$ diverges, while sequentially compact obviously implies closeness. On the other hand, assuming $A$ is closed and bounded, we may first find a convergent subsequence $(x_{n_k})$ by Bolzano-Weierstrass, and since $A$ is closed, we have the limit of $x_{n_k}$ in $A$.

Compact Set

Actually, there is another equivalent criteria for compactness, albeit in completely different form. We say a set $U$ is open whenever for each $x \in U$, there exists some $r \gt 0$ where $(c - r, c + r) \subseteq U$. Note that open-ness remains holds for arbitrary union and finite intersection of open sets. Interestingly, $A$ is closed iff its complement $A^c$ is open. Intuitively speaking, both means that elements of $A^c$ cannot be approached arbitrarily close by sequences in $A$. We say a collection of open sets $\{ J_\alpha : \alpha \in \Lambda \}$ where as an open cover of $A$ if $A \subseteq \bigcup_{\alpha \in \Lambda} J_\alpha$.

In fact, Heine-Borel Theorem stats that any open cover of a closed bounded interval admits a finite subcover. The proof is essentially by binary search on the intervals that does not have a finite subcover, but ultimately we have $\bigcap I_n = \{ c \}$ without a finite subcover, which is absurd. Inspired by this, we say a set $A \subset \mathbb{R}$ is compact iff for any open cover we can find a finite subcover.

Turns out in $\mathbb{R}$, (1) compactness (finite subcover), (2) sequential compactness (convergent subsequence), (3) closed and bounded are equivalent conditions! We have previously see (2) and (3) are equivalent. To show (1) implies (3), assume $A$ is compact. Note that compactness implies bounded by consider any finite subcover, and if $(x_n) \rightarrow L \not\in A$, then for every $a \in A$ there exists $\delta_a \gt 0$ where $L \not\in J_a = (a - \delta_a, a + \delta_a)$. By compactness, $\bigcup \{ J_a \}$ admits a finite subcover, so $L$ must not be a cluster point, contradiction. Finally, to show (3) implies (1), assume $A$ is closed and bounded, and there is an open cover $\bigcup\{ J_\alpha \}$ of $A$. Note $A \subset [a, b]$ for some closed interval since $A$ is bounded, and for any $a \not\in A$ there exists $\delta_a \gt 0$ where $(a - \delta_a, a + \delta_a) \subset A^c$ since $A^c$ is open. Thus the open cover $\bigcup\{ J_\alpha \} \cup \bigcup \{ (a - \delta_a, a + \delta_a) \}$ admits a finite subcover of $[a, b]$ and henceforth of $A$.

Note that compactness and sequential compactness is equivalent in $\mathbb{R}$ (or more generally metric space) but not for general topological space.

Cauchy Sequence

Next, we will introduce another criterion for determining convergence of a sequence. A sequence $(x_n)$ is called Cauchy iff $$ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists N \in \mathbb{N} \quad \forall m, n \ge N \quad |x_m - x_n| \lt \varepsilon$$ It does look quite similar to the definition of the convergence, but here the limit $L$ is not involved. In fact, a sequence is Cauchy iff it is convergent - Clearly convergence imply Cauchy. Since Cauchy implies bounded, by Bolzano-Weierstrass there exists a subsequence $(x_{n_k}) \rightarrow L$. Thus, $(x_n) \rightarrow L$ as well as $(x_n)$ is Cauchy.

For obvious sake, we can extend all the above definitions from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{R}^m$ trivially.

Functions

Our next focus is on functions. Consider a function $f: A \subset \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, what analytic properties can we deduce for $f$?

Function Limit

We first define the limit of the function. For $c \in D(A)$ a cluster point of $A$, we write $$ \lim_{x \rightarrow c} f(x) = L $$ Which means when $x$ approaches $c$, the value $f(x)$ approaches $L$. Formally using the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formulation, it means $$ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists \delta \gt 0 \quad \forall y \in A \quad 0 \lt |y - c| \lt \delta \implies |f(y) - L| \lt \varepsilon $$ Equivalently, we have the sequential criteria: $$ \forall (x_n) \subset A \setminus \{ c \} \quad (x_n) \rightarrow c \implies (f(x_n)) \text{ converges } $$ It is more obvious that $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ implies sequential criteria; For the opposite direction, note that all limits are same since we can "merge" sequences $(x_n), (y_n) \rightarrow c$ into one by $(x_1, y_1, x_2, y_2, \dots)$. If the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ criteria does not hold, then there exists a $\varepsilon \gt 0$ where $(x_n) \rightarrow c$ but $|f(y) - L| \ge \varepsilon$, which is absurd.

Similar to the case for sequence limit, we may compute the limit for $f \pm g$, $f \cdot g$ and $f / g$ (where $0 \not\in g(A)$ and limit not $0$) intuitively, and the proof is also directly implied by the sequential criteria.

We may define some extension to the above definitions for function limits. For example, by $\lim_{x \rightarrow c} f(x) \rightarrow \infty$ we actually means $$ \forall M \gt 0 \quad \exists \delta \gt 0 \quad 0 \lt |y - c| \lt \delta \implies f(x) \gt M $$ Or by $\lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} f(x) \rightarrow L$ we means $$ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists R \quad \forall x \gt R \quad |f(x) - L| \lt \varepsilon$$

Continuity

Next, continuity. What does it mean by $f$ is continuous at $c \in A$? That means $$ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists \delta \gt 0 \quad \forall x \in A \quad |x - c| \lt \delta \implies |f(x) - f(c)| \lt \varepsilon$$ Note that for non limit point $x$, the condition vacuously holds. The reason why we only consider $c \in A$ is due to, well, we need $f(c)$ to be well-defined. In fact, continuity is related to open sets. The condition that $f$ is continuous on $A$ is equivalent to that for all open $V \subset \mathbb{R}$, then $f^{-1}(V)$ is also open. Also, for $c \in D(A) \cap A$ and $f$ continuous at $c$, we have $\lim_{x \rightarrow c} f(x) = f(c)$. Sequential criteria holds similarly; whereas for $f, g$ continuous, we have $f \pm g$, $f \cdot g$, $f/g$, $f \circ g$ continuous as well whenever compatible.

Here comes an important theorem - the Extreme Value Theorem, which states that a continuous function $f$ defined on a compact set $A$ are bounded and have extreme values. The EVT can be proven via either definitions for compactness - (1) for all sequence in $A$, there exists a subsequence with limit in $A$; (2) every open cover of $A$ admits a finite subcover.

First, with the sequential definition. Suppose $f$ is unbounded, then we can find $(x_n) \subset A$ where $(x_n) \rightarrow \infty$ or $-\infty$, which no convergent subsequence can be found, so $f$ must be bounded. so $L = \sup_{x \in A} \{ f(x) \}$ is well defined, and there exists $(x_n)$ such that $(f(x_n)) \rightarrow L$. We invoke the definition of sequential compactness again and we have $(x_{n_k}) \rightarrow a \in A$. Since $f$ is continuous, we have $f(a) = L$ and we are done.

With the open cover definition we can prove similarly. First consider the open cover $A \subset \left\{ (x - \delta_x, x + \delta_x) \right\}$ where $|y - x| \lt \delta_x \implies |f(y) - f(x)| \lt \varepsilon$ for some fixed $\varepsilon \gt 0$. By the finite subcover we obviously have $f$ bounded. Once again we invoke the axiom of completeness and have $L = \sup_{x \in A} \{ f(x) \}$. If no $a \in A$ makes $f(a) = L$, then we can once again consider the open cover $\{ (x - \delta_x, x + \delta_x) \}$ where this time $|y - x| \lt \delta_x \implies |f(y) - f(x)| \lt |L - f(x)|$. Pass to the finite subcover, trivial to see $L$ cannot be the supremum.

Turns out compactness is preserved by continuous functions as well! Here, we just use the open cover way to prove it. Intuitively, for any open cover of $f(A)$, we can pull it back to be a open cover of $A$, which has a finite subcover; and so mapping them back we have a finite subcover. We say two subsets are homeomorphic if there exists a bijection $f: A \rightarrow B$ where both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are continuous. We also have that for continuous bijection $f: A \rightarrow B$ and $A$ compact, then $f$ is homeomorphism as well, which can be proven from definition.

Finally, we have the Intermediate Value Theorem - Given continuous $f: [a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $f(a) \lt L \lt f(b)$, then there exists $c \in (a, b)$ where $f(c) = L$. One may simply use binary search and nested interval theorem to show $f(c) = \lim f(a_n) = \lim f(b_n)$ and so $f(c) = L$. A corollary to IVT is that continuous functions map intervals to intervals.

Uniform Continuity

Uniform continuity is a stronger condition to continuity - defined as $$ \forall \varepsilon \gt 0 \quad \exists \delta \gt 0 \quad \forall x, y \in A \quad |x - y| \lt \delta \implies |f(x) - f(y)| \lt \varepsilon$$ Which now the $\delta$ is picked for the whole function instead of point-wise. Turns out continuous functions defined on compact set are always uniformly continuous!

With the open cover definition this is trivial, whereas for the sequential compactness, suppose $f$ is not uniformly continuous. Then there exists some $\varepsilon \gt 0$ where for all $\delta \gt 0$, there exists some $x, y \in A$ where $|x - y| \lt \delta$ and $|f(x) - f(y)| \ge \varepsilon$. Select subsequence by sequential compactness twice, we have both $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ converges but $|f(x_n) - f(y_n)| \ge \varepsilon$, contradiction.

With the aid of uniform continuity, we can prove something like the Weierstrass approximation theorem: for every continuous function $f: [0, 1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, we can approximate $f$ with a polynomial $p$ where $\Vert f - p \Vert_{\infty} \lt \varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon$, using a linear combination of Bernstein polynomials $B_n(x) = \sum a_k \binom{n}{k} x^k (1 - x)^{n - k}$. We can approximate continuous functions on compact set with piecewise-linear functions as well - directly implied by $f$ being uniform continuous.

Now, for a continuous function $f : (a, b) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, when can we extend the definition to $[a, b]$? Turns out the following definitions are equivalent: (1) existence of continuous $F: [a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ where $F(x) = f(x)$ for all $x \in (a, b)$; (2) $f$ uniformly continuous on $(a, b)$; and (3) $\lim_{x \rightarrow a^+} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \rightarrow b^-} f(x)$ both exists. All the implications are straight from definitions as you can see.

Lipschitz Continuity

A function $f: A \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is called Lipschitz if $$ \exists C \gt 0 \quad \forall x, y \in A \quad |f(x) - f(y)| \le C|x - y| $$ Clearly Lipschitz is even stronger than uniform continuity. When $0 \lt C \lt 1$, the function $f$ is called a contraction.

For any closed subset $A$ and contraction $f: A \rightarrow A$, we can in fact show the fixed point $f(a) = a$ is unique. How? Simply note that $\{ f^n(a) \}$ is Cauchy and sequence generated by different $a$ must converges to the same limit. This holds more generally in metric spaces.

Monotonous Functions

Without loss of generality, we assume $f$ is an increasing function defined on $A \subset \mathbb{R}$. Define $L(c) = \inf_{x \gt c} f(x)$ and $\ell(c) = \sup_{x \lt c} f(x)$, then if $c$ is right limit we have $L(c) = \lim_{x \rightarrow c^+} f(x)$; and if $c$ is left limit we have $\ell(c) = \lim_{x \rightarrow c^-} f(x)$. Note that the set of discontinuity is actually countable, by investigating with standard techniques.

Limit Supremum and Infinum

We can also define $$\overline{\lim}_{x \rightarrow c} f(x) = \lim_{\delta \rightarrow 0^+} \left( \sup_{0 \lt |x - c| \lt \delta} f(x) \right)$$ And $$\underline{\lim}_{x \rightarrow c} f(x) = \lim_{\delta \rightarrow 0^+} \left( \inf_{0 \lt |x - c| \lt \delta} f(x) \right)$$ For $f$ locally bounded at $c$. Similar to the sequence case, we have $\overline{\lim}_{x \rightarrow c} f(x) = \underline{\lim}_{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ iff $\lim_{x \rightarrow c} f(x)$ exists.

Bounded Variation

Finally we define the total variation of a function $f: [a, b] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ as $$ \Vert f \Vert_{BV} = \sup \left\{ \sum | f(x_k) - f(x_{k - 1}) | : a = x_0 \lt \cdots \lt x_n = b \right\} \lt \infty$$ Where $f$ is said to be of bounded variations. We can write $BV[a, b]$ as the set of all functions of bounded variations.

Clearly $BV[a, b]$ is a vector space, bounded variation implies bounded while monotone / Lipschitz implies bounded variation. In fact, a function is of bounded variation iff it can be written as the difference of two increasing functions, which can be proven via potential functions.
